prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, enabling atomic clocks of unprecedented accuracy

statement.case_for: I keep B009, Katori and Ye, as the whole configuration, and my reasons are the same as in round 1 but I can now state them more sharply after reading the other seven statements. The new element is a single physical idea: choose the wavelength of the trapping light so that the light shift of the two clock levels is equal, and the atoms can then be held tightly, with no Doppler or recoil broadening, while thousands of them are interrogated at once. This is not the comb and not an ion in a Paul trap. It also was not obvious that it would work, because a trap light field strong enough to hold atoms normally perturbs the transition far more than the accuracy one wants. The test I apply to a result is whether independent laboratories, using different species, reproduce it and agree quantitatively with a theory of the systematic shifts. Here Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several countries do that at the 10^-18 level, and the shifts (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarizability, collisions and spin-exchange) are understood well enough to be corrected rather than merely bounded. The physics that came out is real physics: gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, constraints on drifting constants, and the many-body behaviour of a degenerate Fermi gas inside a clock. For credit I would put it plainly in the record: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first realization, and Ye's group carried it to record accuracy and stability and found the many-body side of the clock. Those are two separable contributions of the kind the committee has honoured before.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the objection that every one of us raised, so I will not pretend it is settled by our agreement. My answer is the citation: it must name the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation as the new element and must not rest on clock accuracy in general, on the comb, or on the redefinition of the second, which is a consequence and could still be delayed. Eriksson is right that I should be more careful about 2012 than about 2005, since the Al+ ion clock covers some of the same ground of accuracy. I accept that, and it is a reason for the wording, not a reason to hold the prize back. A second weakness is credit. Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Ludlow and Oates at NIST, Takamoto, PTB and the theory of magic wavelengths all matter, and a two-name citation leaves them out. I think the discovery and the programme that made it a metrological instrument are separable in the way the committee needs, but this rests on my recollection of the priority sequence and I would like it checked by outside experts before the vote. Finally, I concede to Johansson and Danielsson that no departure from known physics has been seen. The prize would be for a new capability that has already produced physics, not for a new law.

responses.point: Asked whether Jun Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme (comb-linked spectroscopy, spin-exchange physics), and whether Hall's 2005 prize affects how his share is framed.
responses.response: I will answer as an atomic physicist, with the caveat that I did not do this work. I would not frame Ye's share around the comb at all. Hall's 2005 prize and Ye's comb work belong to the earlier citation, and honouring that again would be exactly the double counting you and Eriksson fear. What I would credit Ye with is specific to the lattice clock: bringing the strontium lattice clock to a regime where systematic effects were evaluated at the 10^-18 level, and showing that collisions and spin-exchange in a degenerate Fermi gas are part of the clock physics and not a nuisance. Those results would not exist without the lattice idea. So I would word his part by the lattice clock and not by JILA in general, and I would not attach Hall's role to the allocation. If the outside reviewers tell us that the evidence for Ye's lattice-specific role is thinner than I believe, that is a real objection, and it would be better to learn it before the ballot.

responses.point: Is less relaxed about the 2012 ion-clock prize than about 2005, and says the citation must be framed around the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation and not around clock accuracy in general.
responses.response: On the citation I agree with you completely and I have changed my own wording to follow it. My round-1 citation led with the 10^-18 level, and you and Pearce have convinced me that it should not: a number can be improved on, and it invites the reading that this is a prize for the best clock. The distinction from 2012 is physical. A single trapped ion is controlled one quantum system at a time and pays for that with a long averaging time. The lattice clock gets its statistics from many neutral atoms, which only works because the magic wavelength removes the lattice perturbation, and that brings the Fermi-gas many-body shifts into the problem. I do not claim that this makes the overlap vanish. I claim that it is a different principle, and that the committee can say so in a sentence. If you still find after this that three metrology prizes in twenty years is too many, I would want to hear it as a judgement about the Academy's balance and not as a scientific point, because the scientific point I believe is answered.

responses.point: Ranked the lattice clock sixth for overlap and set the citation on magic-wavelength trapping, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, while asking for it to be a distinct conceptual step.
responses.response: Your citation anchors on magic-wavelength trapping, and I think that is the right anchor, better than my own. I would keep the sentence about uncertainty out of the citation or put it second, for the reason above. On your worry that a widely expected prize crowds out less familiar work, I would turn it around: the candidates that I value most are those where agreement between independent measurements can be checked by anyone, and here it is checked in international clock comparisons, which are a more demanding test than most fields can offer. That is a reason to prefer it, not a reason to suspect it. On active matter, I cannot judge it as you can, but you have yourself noted that the quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is partial, and I would not want to set it ahead of a result that has been reproduced in many laboratories.

responses.point: Asked whether the redefinition of the second and the new-physics searches count as realised or still prospective impact, and noted a year of his PhD in John Hall's lab in Boulder.
responses.response: Realised and prospective impact should be kept apart in the citation, as you suggest. What is already realised is the performance, the comparisons between laboratories, the redshift measured over millimetres and the bounds on drifts of constants. The redefinition and the searches for dark matter are prospective, and I would leave both out of the text, so that a delay in the redefinition cannot make the citation look premature. On your link to Hall, I do not think it matters for B009 and I am glad you put it on the record. Its relevance is rather to the point I answered for Pearce, that Hall's work is the 2005 prize and should not shape Ye's share here. I also agree with you on B001: we both keep it as a reserve and I would not pair it with the clock, given the unresolved position of Chu.

responses.point: Asked whether the invention credit rests on Katori's proposal and first demonstration or also on Ye's accuracy and stability milestones, and wants the history checked.
responses.response: I would split it as I did above: the invention is Katori's, in the sense of the magic-wavelength idea and the first demonstration of a lattice clock, and the accuracy and stability milestones and the many-body physics are Ye's. I think a citation can say both by using 'invention and realization', as it does, without claiming that both men invented the same thing. But I share your wish to see the order of the milestones checked. I am recalling the priority sequence among RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST from memory and a theorist is not the right person to settle it. I would support a request to outside experts on exactly that question before the final ballot, and my support for the two-name credit stands on the condition that it comes back as I expect.

responses.point: Said a prize about better numbers risks looking incremental, and that the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing right.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and not with the second. A prize about better numbers would be incremental, which is why I want the citation to say what is new in principle. But I would not treat the redefinition of the second as supporting the timing, because it is still prospective, and if the committee leans on it and it slips, the prize looks premature. The timing argument I rely on is simpler: the invention dates from the early 2000s, the clocks have been reproduced and compared for more than a decade, and the physics that came from them is already in the literature. That is mature without the redefinition.

uncertainties: Whether outside experts confirm that Katori's proposal and first realization and Ye's accuracy and many-body contributions are separable in the way I describe, and whether the roles of Lemonde and SYRTE, Ludlow and Oates, Takamoto and PTB change that; I am recalling the priority sequence from memory.

Whether colleagues with a low opening rank (Eriksson and Mehlig) and Pearce regard the 2005 and 2012 overlap as a reason to hold the prize back even after the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice; this is a judgement about the Academy's balance that I cannot settle alone.

Whether any second part pairs cleanly with B009 under the three-name limit. I looked again and found none: B010 requires choosing three of four names, B001 omits Chu, and the others have their own open credit questions. I am therefore not proposing one.
If B009 is set aside, my reserve is B010 but the choice of three of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller would need work, and I am not sure it is ready either.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of them is involved in B009. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and know of no conflict for B009. For the reserves B010 and B001 I have no direct connection to the named people, only membership of the same broad atomic-physics community. No change from round 1, and I note that Kroll's year in Hall's lab and Johansson's B008 connection are matters for them and for the chair, not ties of mine.
